title: Games, Full Abstraction and Full Completeness

summaries.example: Imagine two programs that both make a red light turn on. We can say they act the same from the outside, even if they are built differently inside. A program's meaning can also be described by what its parts mean. Full abstraction asks whether these two ways of describing programs agree. Game semantics imagines a program and its surroundings taking turns: the surroundings ask for information, and the program answers.
summaries.summary: This entry asks how we should explain the meaning of computer programs. One approach studies what happens when a program runs. Another gives programs mathematical meanings, ideally by combining the meanings of their parts. These approaches create ways of deciding when two programs count as equivalent. Full abstraction is the goal of making the mathematical and behavioral judgments match. The entry studies why this goal is difficult for PCF, a small language with functions, numbers, truth values, and recursion. A standard mathematical model can describe a parallel operation that PCF itself cannot define. Researchers therefore developed more detailed accounts of sequential computation, including stable functions, sequential algorithms, and games. In game semantics, a program is represented by a strategy for answering an environment's moves. The entry also explains full completeness, a stronger idea from the connection between proofs and programs: every suitable mathematical object should come from a proof or program.
key_ideas: Programs can be understood by their behavior when they run or by mathematical descriptions of them.
A context is a program with an empty spot where another program can be placed.
A good meaning should respect how programs are put together.
Some mathematical descriptions allow parallel behavior that the small language PCF cannot express.
Games and strategies model computation as interaction between a program and its environment.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help computer scientists decide whether a mathematical model really captures a programming language. They also clarify what it means for two programs to be interchangeable, how program parts fit together, and how a program interacts with its environment. The work connects programming, logic, mathematics, and the study of proofs.

important_terms.definition: A set of rules for explaining what a program means or how it works.
Building the meaning of a whole program from the meanings of its smaller parts.
Treating two programs as the same when no allowed surrounding program can tell them apart.
A test of whether a mathematical description and actual program behavior agree about which programs are the same.
A way to describe computing as a back-and-forth exchange of questions and answers.

summaries.example: Consider a function that returns true when at least one of two boolean inputs is true. A mathematical model may allow it to inspect both inputs in parallel, so it can return true when one input is already true while the other has not produced an answer. In call-by-name PCF, evaluation proceeds sequentially, and this parallel-or operation is not definable. Thus the standard denotational model distinguishes some terms that no PCF context can distinguish. This is a failure of full abstraction, not necessarily a failure of computational adequacy.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates how formal semantics can capture the meaning of programs. Operational semantics describes execution and observable results. Denotational semantics maps phrases to mathematical objects, often in domains ordered by amount of information. When this mapping is compositional, the meaning of a compound phrase is calculated from its parts, and denotational equivalence is preserved by contexts. Observational equivalence instead asks whether any context can distinguish two phrases. Full abstraction requires these equivalences to coincide. Computational adequacy is a weaker requirement linking successful evaluation with denotation. For PCF, the usual continuous domain model is computationally adequate but fails full abstraction. Its higher-type functions include parallel-or, whose output can depend on either input becoming true, even though the language's sequential evaluation cannot define that operation. Other models try to describe sequentiality more accurately through stability, sequentiality indices, concrete data structures, and sequential algorithms. Game semantics shifts attention to interaction: games specify legal questions and answers, while strategies specify a program's responses. More refined strategies, constrained by innocence and well-bracketing, characterize the relevant PCF denotations. Full completeness provides a related, stronger form of definability in proof semantics: every suitable morphism or semantic object should arise from a proof.
key_ideas: Operational semantics follows execution, while denotational semantics assigns mathematical objects to phrases.
Compositionality supports substitution: replacing a phrase with an equivalent one should preserve the meaning of every suitable context.
Computational adequacy is weaker than full abstraction: it connects evaluation with denotation but does not guarantee that all contextual distinctions are represented.
The continuous model of PCF is adequate but not fully abstract because it contains parallel-or, which PCF cannot define under the relevant sequential evaluation.
Attempts to capture sequentiality include stable functions, sequential functions, concrete data structures, and sequential algorithms.

Game semantics represents programs as strategies in structured interactions; innocence and well-bracketing help characterize PCF computations and yield an intensional full-abstraction result for suitable types.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction between behavior and mathematical meaning matters whenever we use models to reason about software. A model can be correct about termination yet contain distinctions or functions unavailable in the language. Full abstraction gives a demanding standard for avoiding this mismatch. Game semantics also offers a detailed account of higher-order computation, showing how interaction and evaluation order can be represented mathematically.

important_terms.definition: An interpretation that assigns program phrases mathematical denotations, usually in structures such as domains, while respecting program-building operations.
An interpretation based on execution: what value a program produces, if evaluation terminates.
The property that a whole phrase's meaning is determined by the meanings of its components and the way they are combined.
Equivalence in which two phrases have the same denotation in a semantic model.
Equivalence in which no program context can distinguish two phrases by their observable results.
The condition that denotational and observational equivalence coincide.
A mathematical structure ordered by information, with a least or undefined element and limits for increasing approximations.
A typed functional language with arithmetic and boolean primitives and a fixed-point operator, used to study semantic models.

summaries.example: Suppose two versions of a calculator program both return 7 whenever they are placed into any of the classroom's test programs. From the outside, they are observationally equivalent. A denotational model might also assign them the same mathematical object. Full abstraction asks whether these judgments always agree. The difficulty appears when a model permits a calculator to check two unfinished calculations at once, while the programming language only checks one calculation after another.
summaries.summary: The entry explores how to give programming languages precise meanings and how to compare different meanings. Operational semantics describes what happens during execution, including whether a program terminates with a value. Denotational semantics assigns mathematical objects to program phrases. Compositionality says that the meaning of a whole phrase depends systematically on the meanings of its parts. This makes denotational equivalence stable under contexts, where a context is a larger phrase with a hole. Observational equivalence is based instead on what contexts can detect. Full abstraction is achieved when these two forms of equivalence coincide. The entry uses PCF, a typed language with functions, numbers, booleans, and recursion, to show why this is hard. Its standard domain model is computationally adequate, but it is not fully abstract: the model contains parallel-or, which can return true if either input is true, even when the other is unfinished. PCF's sequential evaluation cannot define this operation. Later approaches refine the model to represent sequentiality and interaction. Game semantics treats computation as a dialogue between an environment and a program. Games list legal moves, and strategies describe how the program responds. Full completeness is a related idea in the semantics of proofs: every suitable semantic process should correspond to a proof, much as definability asks whether semantic elements come from programs.
key_ideas: There are different ways to interpret a program, and each highlights a different aspect of it.
Contexts represent possible environments in which a program phrase may be used and tested.
A compositional interpretation makes equivalent pieces safely replaceable inside larger phrases.
The standard continuous interpretation of PCF includes parallel-or, but parallel-or is not definable in PCF's sequential evaluation.
Researchers sought models that capture sequential behavior more precisely, including stable and sequential functions.
Game semantics describes programs as strategies in interactions and connects programming-language semantics with logic and proof theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: These questions matter because programmers and computer scientists use mathematical models to predict and explain program behavior. Full abstraction asks a model to be neither too coarse nor too fine about program equivalence. The topic also shows that computation involves more than input and final output: order, partial information, interaction, and the structure of questions and answers can all be significant.

important_terms.definition: A formal account of what expressions or programs mean.
A way to calculate the meaning of a larger program from the meanings of its smaller pieces.
A larger program with a hole that can be filled by an expression.
Treating two expressions as equivalent when every suitable context gives them the same observable result.
The requirement that mathematical equivalence and observational equivalence match.
A semantic model in which elements can represent partial information and increasingly informative approximations.
The possibility that evaluation never reaches a value.
A way to model computation through moves, questions, answers, and response plans.
